Summarize this for an engineer joining tomorrow:

The docs renderer used to rebuild every page on every deploy, which made previews slow and made it hard to tell whether a change was safe. We added a content-hash check at the start of the render path. For each page, the parser reads the markdown, computes a hash of the normalized content and its direct partials, and compares that hash with the value stored from the previous successful render. If the hashes match, the server returns the cached HTML and skips template execution, markdown conversion, and asset fingerprint recomputation for that page. If the hashes differ, the renderer runs as before, writes the new HTML to the cache directory, and updates the hash index in the same transaction so a crash cannot leave HTML and hash out of sync. In production last week, 86% of page requests were cache hits, p95 render time fell from 1.8s to 240ms, and the remaining misses were concentrated on pages that import a shared changelog partial. The open follow-up is to split that partial or give it its own cache key so a changelog edit does not invalidate hundreds of otherwise unchanged pages. Locally, developers can bypass the cache with `DOCS_CACHE=0`, and CI still does a full clean render once per merge to catch stale-cache bugs.

Summarize this incident for a status page audience:

At 14:02 UTC, the payments service started returning timeouts on checkout. On-call saw Redis connection errors from the payments pods in the new private subnet. A network change earlier that morning had updated security groups for the database tier but missed the Redis rules for the payments security group, so new pods could not open port 6379. Existing long-lived connections kept some traffic working for several minutes, which made the failure look intermittent in the first graphs. By 14:18 UTC, connection pools were exhausted and checkout error rates crossed 40% for card payments; ACH was unaffected because it uses a different path. At 14:27 UTC we restored the missing ingress rule, and by 14:35 UTC error rates were declining as pods reconnected. We flushed a stuck retry queue at 14:41 UTC and confirmed successful checkouts across regions by 14:47 UTC. Roughly 2,100 checkout attempts failed or were abandoned during the window. We are adding a pre-deploy check that verifies Redis reachability from payments after any network Terraform change, and we will publish a fuller postmortem by Friday.

Summarize this research note in plain language:

We trained a small classifier to detect unsupported claims in model-written answers. The training set had 4,800 sentences labeled by two annotators, with adjudication on disagreements. On a held-out set of 1,200 sentences, precision was 0.81 and recall was 0.66 for the unsupported class. Most false negatives were hedged claims that used phrases like "it appears" or "some evidence suggests" while still asserting a specific fact without a citation. False positives were often cautious summaries that mentioned a limit of the data. We compared against a prompt-only baseline that asked a larger model to flag unsupported sentences; that baseline reached 0.77 precision and 0.71 recall but cost about 9x more per document at current batch sizes. Next we will add 600 more hedged unsupported examples, retrain, and measure whether recall rises without dropping precision below 0.78. We also plan a slice analysis by domain, because legal and medical sentences currently underperform the average by roughly 8 points of F1.
